newsitem.title: LEBANON: Lebanon opposition MPs blast 1997 proposed budget.
newsitem.headline: Lebanon opposition MPs blast 1997 proposed budget.

text.p: Lebanese opposition MPs ended a debate on the 1997 budget on Saturday by accusing the government of sinking the country in debt while failing to pursue a productive economic policy.

Throughout the four-day debate some deputies questioned the credibility of budget figures and the government's ability to meet a proposed budget deficit of revenue against expenditure of 36 percent after its failure to meet previous targets.

"Every year the government give us budget figures that do not seem sound except on the budget debate day and then lose their meaning and evaporate after the parliament session," Maronite Christian MP Nassib Lahoud told parliament.
The 1996 deficit overran a target of 37.6 percent to 51 percent. In 1994 and 1995, it exceeded targets of 43 percent and 44 percent, reaching 57 and 47 percent respectively.
"I am strongly afraid we might find ourselves next year in the same trap as the deficit widens further," Lahoud added.
Maronite Christian MP Boutros Harb blasted the government for slashing investment spending in the 1997 budget and ignoring the country's productive sectors.

"The government claims that its economic and financial policy aims at providing suitable environments for private sector investment promotion...yet it cuts to half investment spending to reach only 7.4 percent of total spending," he said.
He said the total spending allocated to ministries of industry, agriculture and tourism did not exceed 1.29 percent of a total proposed spending of 6,433 billion pounds ($4 billion).
Another Maronite Christian MP Pierre Dakkash pointed out that "about 40 percent of 1997 proposed spending will go to debt servicing and interest" -- some 100 billion pounds up on last year.
"The budget is unproductive as it stabs industry, ignores agriculture and disables capital by freezing it in treasury bills," Dakkash said.
Leftist Christian MP Najah Wakim said the country's indebtedness had reached a disasterous level. "When they say the public debt has reached 83 percent it is a disaster".

Foreign and net domestic debt have each more than doubled since December 1994. Foreign debt has risen to $1.769 billion from $772 million and net domestic debt to 13,315 billion Lebanese pounds from 6,682 billion.
Total debt reached $10.348 billion at end of December 1996, a figure which according to one parliamentary deputy approaches Lebanon's estimated gross domestic product.
As pro-government deputies dominate the 128-member parliament, the budget is expected to be approved easily during a late night voting session on Saturday.
